6                 IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                    
7                     FOR THE DISTRICT OF ARIZONA                        

8                                                                        

9   BMO Harris Bank NA,                No. CV-22-00547-PHX-DWL           

10              Plaintiff,              ORDER                             

11   v.                                                                   

12   Duncan Corley, et al.,                                               

13              Defendants.                                               
14                                                                        
15        The parties have filed a joint motion to stay, in which they explain that they entered 
16   into a settlement agreement two and a half months ago, “have continuing obligations to 
17   one  another  through  July  4,  2023”  pursuant  to  that  agreement,  and  believe  it  to  be 
18   “necessary” that the Court retain jurisdiction until that date because “breach by either party 
19   of the terms of the Agreement . . . would require intervention of the Court.”  (Doc. 36.) 
20        As a preliminary matter, the parties should have filed a notice of settlement long 
21   ago, as one of the terms of the Court’s scheduling order is that “[t]he parties shall promptly 
22   notify the Court if settlement is reached.”  (Doc. 28 at 7.)         
23        Furthermore, it is not “necessary” for the Court to retain jurisdiction over this 
24   matter.  Although it is true that a federal court may retain jurisdiction over a case that has 
25   settled, this is not the usual approach.  Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 
26   375, 381-82 (1994) (“[A]utomatic jurisdiction over such contracts is in no way essential to 
27   the  conduct  of  federal-court  business.    If  the  parties wish to  provide  for  the  court’s 
28   enforcement of a dismissal-producing settlement agreement, they can seek to do so.”).  A 
1   request for the Court to retain jurisdiction while the parties fulfill settlement obligations is 
2   an assertion that the Court should exercise “ancillary jurisdiction” over a dismissed suit, 
3   which the Court can do “to manage its proceedings, vindicate its authority, and effectuate 
4   its decrees,” so long as the Court expressly reserves jurisdiction.  Id. at 379-80.  Generally, 
5   when a case is dismissed, the dismissal order “is in no way flouted or imperiled by [an] 
6   alleged breach of the settlement agreement.”  Id. at 380.  However, the situation is “quite 
7   different if the parties’ obligation to comply with the terms of the settlement agreement [is] 
8   made part of the order of dismissal—either by separate provision (such as a provision 
9   ‘retaining jurisdiction’ over the settlement agreement) or by incorporating the terms of the 
10   settlement agreement in the order.”  Id. at 381.1  In that situation, breach of the settlement 
11   agreement  is  a  violation  of  a  court  order,  and  “ancillary  jurisdiction  to  enforce  the 
12   agreement . . . therefore exist[s].”  Id.                            
13        “[I]f parties wish to have a district court retain jurisdiction to enforce a settlement, 
14   they must apply for that relief and allow the court to make a reasoned determination as to 
15   whether retention is appropriate.”  Cross Media Mktg. Corp. v. Budget Mktg., Inc., 319 F. 
16   Supp. 2d 482, 483 (S.D.N.Y. 2004).  A district court may “properly decline to retain 
17   jurisdiction where the administration of a settlement threatened to impose undue burdens 
18   on it.”  Id.  See also Camacho v. City of San Luis, 359 Fed. App’x 794, 798 (9th Cir. 2009) 
19   (“[I]t was the court’s prerogative not to retain jurisdiction over any disputes raised by the 
20   [settlement].”).                                                     

21   1    This is a “consent decree” or “consent judgment.”  “A consent decree is no more 
    than a settlement that contains an injunction.”  Fed. Trade Comm’n v. Enforma Nat. Prod., 
22   Inc., 362 F.3d 1204, 1218 (9th Cir. 2004) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted).  
    In contrast, “[w]hen the settlement involves no injunctive relief but simply the payment of 
23   money, the often-used term is ‘consent judgment.’”  Anthony DiSarro, Six Decrees of 
    Separation: Settlement Agreements and Consent Orders in Federal Civil Litigation, 60 
24   Am. U. L. Rev. 275, 277 n.2 (2010).  In other words, a “consent judgment” is merely a run-
    of-the-mill monetary settlement that carries the full force of a court order.  The order can 
25   be enforced through the Court’s contempt power, id. at 277-88, and it ensures that the 
    parties can return to federal court to enforce the settlement, id. at 293-95.  Where a consent 
26   decree includes non-monetary terms providing injunctive relief and the issuing court has 
    been involved in the matter, the judge’s familiarity with the case makes a return to federal 
27   court beneficial.  Id. at 295.  A consent judgment, on the other hand, merely involves the 
    payment of money and “does not implicate any issues within the expertise of federal 
28   judges.”  Id.                                                        
 1          Here,  the  parties  “have  not  attempted  to  explain  why  the  Court’s  continued 
  ||  jurisdiction is required” or “why they would be unable to achieve adequate relief in state 
3 ||  court—which is the traditional avenue for seeking relief following the breach of a contract” 
       if a breach of the settlement obligations were to occur.  Sw.  Fair Hous.  Council Inc.  v. 
  ||  Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement Dist., 2020 WL 1659915, *3 (D. Ariz. 2020).  The 
6 ||  Court will afford the parties another opportunity to establish that the Court should retain 
      ancillary jurisdiction over this settled action. 
8          Finally, even if the parties persuade the Court to retain jurisdiction over this matter 
  ||  while the parties fulfill their settlement obligations, the appropriate procedure would be to 
10 ||  dismiss the action but retain jurisdiction, not to keep the already-settled action open and 
11 ||  stayed.  A stay is a pause in active litigation, and the party seeking a stay “must make out 
12 ||  aclear case of hardship or inequity in being required to go forward.”  Landis v. N. Am. Co., 
13 ||  299 U.S. 248, 255 (1936).  This case having settled, there will be no going forward at all, 
      and thus there is no active litigation to pause.  The proper next step is dismissal.  Hammond 
15 ||  Clock Co v. Schiff, 293 U.S. 529 (1934) (dismissal warranted after settlement). 
16          Accordingly, IT IS ORDERED that the motion to stay (Doc. 36) is denied. 
17          IT  IS  FURTHER  ORDERED  that,  this  case  having  settled,  all  hearings  and 
18 |}  deadlines are vacated. 
19          IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the parties shall, by February 24, 2023, file a 
  ||  stipulation of dismissal.  If, after review of this order and relevant case law, the parties 
      believe the Court should retain ancillary jurisdiction over the dismissed action, they may 
  ||  include argument in support of this request in their stipulation. 
23          IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that if the parties fail to file a stipulation of dismissal 
  ||  seeking retention of ancillary jurisdiction, the action will be dismissed without retention of 
25 ||  jurisdiction, and the Clerk of Court shall terminate this action without further order of the 
26 ||  Court. 
27          Dated this 13th day of February, 2023.              _ 
28                                                         
                                                        Dominic W.  Lanza 
                                          3.       United States District Judge
